name: type-safe-builder
intent: Constrain object construction through type-level stages so that every required step is performed, in a legal order, before the finished object can be obtained: each step is its own type that exposes only the next step, and only the final stage offers build().
problem: Required construction steps are ordered and unskippable in the domain (credentials before transport, method before URL before body, schema before table), but the builder that assembles the object accepts its setters in any order and exposes build() from the first call: a caller can build a half-initialized object, and the ordering rule survives only as documentation or as a runtime exception thrown far from the mistake.
context: Applies when construction has a small, fixed, statically known sequence of required steps plus some optional ones, and when a wrongly ordered or incomplete construction is expensive (wire protocols, credential and connection setup, generated API clients, security-relevant configuration, test fixtures that must name their tenant). It needs a language with usable static types or a type checker: interfaces/per-step classes, generics or phantom state, or at least a checker that rejects the wrong next call. Where the language already requires every non-default argument at a single call site (Kotlin, Scala, Swift, Python, Ruby), the pattern's guarantee is usually obtained without any builder at all.
benefits: Misuse is rejected before the program runs: an omitted or out-of-order step does not compile (or fails the type checker) instead of producing a half-initialized object at run time.
The API documents its own protocol: only the legal next operations are visible to completion, so 'what do I call now?' is answered by the tooling rather than by prose.
An ordering rule that was a comment becomes an enforced contract, which removes defensive 'you must call X first' checks and the tests for the impossible sequence.

Intermediate states are unrepresentable for callers: each step hands back exactly the type of the next stage, so the product cannot be obtained early and the builder cannot be resumed from a stale reference.
Each stage is a separate, small collaborator, which makes construction easier to test and to log step by step; repeatable optional steps can be kept on a self-returning final stage.
Because build() is the only way to the product, the result can be made immutable and validated once, with no setters left over from the construction phase.
tradeoffs: The step set is frozen into the interface/type structure: adding, removing or merging a step rewrites the affected stage types and every call site in the chain (the compiler finds them, but the diff is wide and the public API changes).

The construction must be written as one fluent expression: a caller cannot keep a half-built builder in a variable without naming an intermediate stage type, so loops and conditionals around individual steps force helper functions or lose the guarantee.

Dependencies that run opposite to step order are impossible: an earlier step cannot read data produced by a later one, so a workflow whose next step depends on run-time values needs an interface graph with several successors or a runtime state machine.

Type multiplication: N steps means N public types plus one non-public implementation; for three or four fields with no ordering requirement this is boilerplate that named or defaulted constructor parameters avoid entirely.
Presence is not validity: the staging proves that a step ran, never that its value is sensible, so cross-field and value validation still has to be written in the terminal step and can be forgotten.
Diagnostics for a skipped step read as 'no such method' (or an unsatisfied constraint in the template-based forms) on an intermediate type, which newcomers frequently misdiagnose as a broken API.
The fluent chain hides the receiver: every call returns a different type, so 'find usages' no longer shows the builder's whole surface and readers must know the stage sequence to follow the code.

Stage types leak into the public API surface, so the pattern raises the API's maintenance cost even when the object being built is small, and loosening the staging later is a breaking change for callers.

participants.responsibility: Declares exactly the operations legal at this point of the sequence and returns the next stage's type from each of them; the stage type is the machine-checked precondition of the following step.
The single non-public class/struct that implements every stage type, accumulates the partially built state, and is returned as a stage type by each transition.

The only public way into the sequence - a static factory, companion function or smart constructor - returning the first stage; the product's constructor stays private so no caller can start mid-chain.
The last stage, which carries build()/the conversion to the product and performs the cross-field validation that presence and order cannot express.
The object being constructed; it is created only from a complete builder state and is typically immutable, with no construction-related setters left on it.
The compiler or static checker: method resolution on the stage type is what rejects a skipped or repeated step, so the guarantee exists at build time rather than at run time.

use_cases: HTTP/SQL client APIs where method, target and payload form a fixed protocol and executing early is the classic misuse (request builders, query DSLs).
Connection, credential and TLS configuration where the endpoint and secrets must be supplied before a transport is opened and build() acquires the resource.
Generated or framework-adjacent client APIs consumed by other teams: the staged chain gives external callers an API that can only be misused by writing code that does not compile.
Test-data factories and fixture DSLs, where a forgotten required attribute should be a build error rather than a null in a later assertion.
Cloud and infrastructure configuration objects (buckets, functions, clusters) where a missing required property must be caught before deployment, not by the provider at apply time.
Objects whose construction includes one exactly-once action (opening a socket, reserving a buffer) followed by repeatable optional steps (headers, tags, abilities).

JabRef generates its test-configuration builders with Jilt's @Builder(style = BuilderStyle.STAGED_PRESERVING_ORDER) (architecture decision 0054), so a linked-file test cannot compile unless every required parameter of BibTestConfiguration is supplied in declaration order - a named production adoption of the staged form for the fixture-factory use case.

The Jilt annotation processor makes this pattern a library's core product for Java: @Builder(style = STAGED) generates one interface per required property plus a terminal build() from an annotated constructor, with @Opt marking optional properties that group onto the final stage.

Embedded Rust crates built to the official Embedded Rust Book's 'Typestate Programming' chapter use consuming transitions (into_foo() consumes FooBuilder) so a half-configured object cannot be obtained from the builder and the builder cannot be reused after the terminal transition.
avoid_when: The object has a few fields and no ordering requirement: a constructor with named/default parameters, an options object or a plain builder is simpler - the idiomatic single-call form in Kotlin, Scala, Swift, Python and Ruby already rejects missing required data.
Only presence matters, not order: C# 11 required members, a typed-builder derive in Rust, or a validating constructor give the same guarantee with a fraction of the API surface.
The next step depends on run-time data (user input, a value fetched from a service): model the state as an enum or state machine and branch - the type system cannot see runtime values.
The object is deserialized from a payload: a schema validator plus a smart constructor is the right tool; a staged chain would only duplicate the schema in types.
The construction happens once in one place: the ceremony costs more than a documented function signature, so inline the steps.
Steps are performed by different actors at different times (a multi-session wizard): persist explicit progress state instead of encoding it in types.
anti_patterns: A staged builder around a three-field value with no ordering constraint: pure ceremony, and the stage types are now part of the public API forever.
Leaking the implementation class, a public constructor or the raw stage types so callers can start mid-chain or hold a half-built builder in a variable.
Re-checking required members in every setter instead of once in build(), which duplicates rules and still cannot express cross-field constraints.

Encoding a data-dependent workflow as a type-level chain and then casting or unwrapping intermediate stages at run time to recover a variable sequence - the guarantee is erased exactly where it was needed.
Treating the staging as validation: it proves a step ran, not that the data is correct, so an unvalidated build() produces a well-formed but wrong object.
Leaving fluent setters on the product after build(), which reintroduces mutation and undoes the immutability the staged construction was supposed to deliver.
design_principles: Make illegal states unrepresentable: each stage is a type, so an incomplete sequence has no build() to call and a repeated step has no method to call it with.
Fail fast at the earliest possible moment: the type checker rejects the bad sequence before the program runs.
Interface segregation: a stage type exposes only the operations legal at that point, hiding both earlier and later steps.
Encapsulation at the entry point: a private constructor plus one static factory keep the first stage the only way into the sequence.
Single responsibility: each stage owns one step of the protocol; the implementation class is the only place that knows the whole sequence.
Design by contract: the stage type is the next step's precondition and the returned type is its postcondition, both machine-checked.
best_practices: Return the next stage's type from every step method and declare build()/the product conversion only on the terminal stage.
Keep the constructor private and the implementation class (and, in template-based forms, the stage markers) non-public, so callers cannot start mid-sequence or forge a stage.
Validate once in build(): presence and order come from the stage types; value and cross-field checks belong in the terminal step.
Model optional or repeatable groups as a self-returning final stage or an extended interface, so optional calls remain available without re-opening required steps.
Avoid holding intermediate stages in variables unless the language has consuming transitions; write the chain as one expression or expose a helper function per branch point.
Prove the guarantee with compile-fail tests (trybuild, @ts-expect-error, commented-out non-compiling calls) - a passing test suite cannot show that a skipped step is rejected.
Name the steps in the domain language of the workflow so the staging doubles as API documentation.
Choose the staged form only when the order is a real invariant; otherwise prefer the language's idiomatic single-call construction.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Builder (Creational Patterns): the originating catalog for separating construction from representation, whose step-by-step interface this pattern tightens with type-level staging.
Bloch, Effective Java, 3rd edition (2018), Item 2: 'Consider a builder when faced with many constructor parameters' - the builder form that the staged variant specializes.
